newsitem.title: FRANCE: New Bank of France council to remain cautious.
newsitem.headline: New Bank of France council to remain cautious.

text.p: The Bank of France on Thursday holds its first policy-setting council meeting since the appointment of two new members, amid speculation their arrival will tilt the central bank towards faster rate cuts.

Jean-Rene Bernard and Pierre Guillen joined the nine-member Monetary Policy Council on January 3, replacing Jean Boissonnat and Bruno de Maulde, and many believe they tipped the balance towards the "doves", or those who support faster rate cuts.

But economists said even if the balance of power has shifted, the central bank would probably proceed with cautious rate cuts or leave rates unchanged for a while to send a signal that there will be no revolution.
"I don't think they will move, the reshuffle at the council is too fresh," said Eric Chaney, economist at Morgan Stanley in Paris. "The most likely scenario is a larger cut later."

A Reuter poll of economists on Monday showed two-thirds expected the central bank to make a small cut in the intervention rate, which sets the floor for money market rates, to 3.10 percent after the meeting.

Since October 1995 the Bank has followed a policy of steady, cautious reductions in the intervention rate, usually at times when the risk of weakening the franc against the mark were perceived to be low.
Maintaining a strong franc, the so-called "franc fort" policy, has been a cornerstone of France's commitment to European monetary union and a demonstration of its close relationship with Germany.
Bank of France governor Jean-Claude Trichet, a member of the council, is a staunch defender of the policy and until the new appointments was said to have four confirmed allies.
President Jacques Chirac, who has sparred with Trichet in the past, said in December there was no question of abandoning the franc fort policy.
"It would be a rupture of the Franco-German partnership and then we would face a major European crisis," he said.
But ever since Chirac said last July that French rates were too high, the pressure for faster rate cuts -- seen by some as a panacea for France's economic woes -- has mounted.
Since last July the intervention rate has been trimmed just 0.4 of a percentage point to 3.15 percent and the difference between German and French rates has halved to 0.15 of a point.

The reduction hasn't stemmed widespread calls for faster interest rate cuts from politicians, notably the former president Valery Giscard d'Estaing, unions, employers and even members of the Bank of France's inner sanctum.

Chirac's choice of Guillen and Bernard, both nominated by the Economic and Social Council and both known to have personal ties to the president, fuelled the speculation he could now wield more influence over central bank decisions.

Sluggish growth has pushed the unemployment rate to a record 12.7 percent and while most private economists agree with official predictions the economy will accelerate in 1997, they say the jobless rate has yet to reach its peak.
Some economists say shaving a few basis points off the intervention rate would have little impact on the domestic economy, especially if commercial banks keep their base lending rates steady.
"Even a cut of 20 or 25 basis points won't change anything for investment. I don't think it will trigger any rebound in the economy, the work's already been done," Chaney said.
